extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and readers of philosophy of mathematics (graduate level and above)
extracted.subtask_description: A survey and critical assessment of varieties of formalism (game formalism, term formalism, Hilbertian formalism, Carnapian and later versions), their motivations, and the main objections (applicability, metatheory, Gödelian limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Game formalism (mathematics as a game/calculus of uninterpreted symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is treated as a game bringing no ontological commitment to abstract objects: mathematical utterances are strings transformed according to fixed rules and need not refer to anything outside the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterised by treating formulae as well-formed strings with proof rules; correctness is provability within the system. Example: arithmetic modulo 4 where '3+1=0' can be provable in that system. Anti-pattern: treating the 'signs' as only concrete marks (Frege’s straw-man reading). Requires explicit specification of primitive symbols, recursive well-formedness, and proof rules to be rigorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term formalism (expressions refer to symbols themselves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical expressions are meaningful but their singular terms refer to symbols (expression types) rather than to numbers or abstract mathematical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transforms mathematics into a syntactic theory about symbol-types. Challenge: expression-types appear as abstract entities just as problematic as numbers (Gödel’s arithmetisation shows syntax can be modelled within arithmetic). Use when one wants to preserve meaningfulness of expressions while avoiding platonism; anti-pattern: ignoring that types are themselves abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbertian formalism (finitary vs ideal distinction and instrumentalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction between a finitary/contentful sector (sentences express propositions) and an ideal/infinitary sector (treated as uninterpreted formulae); the ideal sector is instrumentally useful if it is a conservative extension of the finitary sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequacy requires showing the ideal sector does not yield new finitary conclusions not reachable finitarily (conservative extension). Hilbert’s programme sought a finitary proof of this conservativity; Gödel’s second theorem undermines this ideal. Use when defending instrumental justification for ideal methods; anti-pattern: assuming ideal sector harmless without a conservativity proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative extension criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal (infinitary) sector is useful only if it conservatively extends the finitary sector—i.e., no finitary conclusion provable using the ideal resources that could not be proved by finitary means alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert’s programme aimed to provide a finitary proof of conservativity. The absence of such a proof (Gödelian obstacles) is a central problem for Hilbertian/formalist justification of ideal methods. Practical implication: to justify using an ideal calculus in empirical applications, one should show (or argue) conservativity or otherwise justify the instrumental use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability requirement (problem of applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory formalist account must explain why mathematics—if merely a calculus of uninterpreted symbols—applies so successfully to empirical phenomena and other parts of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frege’s objection: 'applicability alone elevates arithmetic from a game to the rank of a science.' Formalists must provide an account (e.g., bridge principles, conservative extension, pragmatic utility) showing how uninterpreted systems yield correct empirical inferences. Anti-pattern: dismissing applicability as irrelevant while relying on mathematics in empirical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metatheory problem (formalism’s metatheoretical commitments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalism must confront that its metatheory (proof theory, syntax, metamathematics) itself seems to be a substantial piece of mathematics, apparently committed to abstract, often infinite, objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the metatheory requires appeal to infinite or abstract entities, the formalist’s anti‑platonist motivation is undermined unless one explains how metatheory can be given without ontological commitment (e.g., via concrete proofs, finitism, or other devices). Anti-pattern: ignoring that metatheoretical reasoning import philosophical commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a rigorous game formalist specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A rigorous game formalist should characterise a formal language by specifying primitive symbols, a recursive specification of well-formed formulae, and a rigorous specification of which arrangements count as proofs and what theorems are proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the mechanics for treating mathematics as a formal object. This avoids crude 'marks on paper' caricatures. Example: give grammar for language, formation rules, axioms, and inference rules. Scoring note: completeness of such a specification is a measure of rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuralist reading (formalism as structuralism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalist emphasis that what matters is the behaviour of symbols under combinatorial rules (the structure) rather than their referents; arithmetic is a game with signs whose content is given by their structural role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to block ontological commitment by claiming mathematics is about positions in structures not about objects. Example: Thomae’s view that arithmetic depends on algebraic operators obeying rules. Anti-pattern: conflating structural descriptions with denial of any abstract structure at all (which invites Fregean criticism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tractarian/Wittgensteinian formalist features
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics treated as a calculus of pseudo-propositions (lacking truth-value) and instrumental in non-mathematical inferences; arithmetic grounded in operations/exponents of operators rather than in abstract numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein’s account focuses on mathematics as operation/algorithm and meaning residing in use. Limits: his Tractarian account covers only a fragment (addition identities) and struggles with inequality, induction, and general mathematics. Use cautiously: it offers an anti‑platonist, use-based standard but lacks generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carnap’s Principle of Tolerance (framework relativism)
rubrics_metrics.description: One may adopt any logical/mathematical framework one wishes; differences between frameworks are addressed by regimenting disputes within formal languages or 'frameworks' rather than by substantive metaphysical claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissiveness avoids ontological disputes but raises pragmatic questions: how to choose frameworks for application and how to secure conservativity or applicability. Anti-pattern: assuming freedom to choose frameworks removes the need to justify applicability to empirical science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to account for Gödelian consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A formalist must address Gödel’s incompleteness results: the existence of non‑determinate sentences in sufficiently expressive formal theories and the limitation on a theory proving its own consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses include moving to stronger systems to prove consistency (Carnap), restricting to weaker languages or finitary methods (Hilbertian attempt), or reinterpreting truth/determinacy. Scoring note: adequacy of a formalist position is partly judged by how it handles Gödelian problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carnapian challenge: bridging application and meaning (bridge principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: To connect formal calculi to empirical sentences, one needs bridge principles or definitions (e.g., definitions linking numerals to existence claims) and must ensure such stipulations do not produce disaster when applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnap recognises that formal calculus alone lacks application sentences; so one must add principles linking calculus to application. Anti-pattern: stipulating bridge principles carelessly (e.g., inconsistent or pragmatically disastrous links). Practical guidance: seek conservativity or contentful justificatory results for added principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weir’s concretist/formalist truth condition (truth via concrete derivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical sentence is true if there exists a concrete derivation of a token of it, and false if there exists a concrete derivation of a token of its negation; truth conditions do not appeal to abstract proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields an anti‑platonist truth notion but faces problems like 'concretely undecidable' sentences whose proofs/disproofs are infeasibly long. Requires an account of what counts as a 'concrete proof' (non‑mathematical account). Anti-pattern: equating formal derivability (ideal proofs) with existence of concrete physical derivations without addressing feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitist constraint on formal truth (feasibility/finitism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine formalism with strict finitism so that only feasibly long formulae and proofs exist; statements lacking feasible proof or disproof lack truth value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses concretely undecidable problems by imposing feasibility limits. But abbreviation and representation practices (creating tokens naming arbitrarily large numbers) undermine strict inductive specification of tokens; idealisation seems necessary. Anti-pattern: applying strict finitism without handling abbreviation/abbreviative devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviation/idealisation problem for finitist formalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation allows formation of complex tokens (e.g., numerals naming arbitrarily high numbers) whose subparts will never exist concretely, showing that strict finitist specifications cannot be given inductively; thus idealisation is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows limits of strict finitism: one cannot avoid idealised infinite resources while still doing ordinary mathematical reasoning. Practical implication: formalists must justify permissible idealisations or face incoherence. Anti-pattern: claiming strict finitist formalism is coherent without addressing abbreviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictionalism/formalist consequence-as-consequence criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: On some fictionalist/formalist views, mathematical truths are just consequences of a stipulated theory; consequence can be read syntactically (derivability) or modally, and the choice affects whether the view counts as formalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary Leng-style fictionalism reads consequence modally rather than syntactically, and so is not a straightforward formalism. Weir and other formalists reading consequence as syntactic derivability make mathematics truth-dependent on derivability. Evaluate positions by how they read 'consequence' and whether that reading supports anti‑platonism and applicability.
